Pursuers
pŭr-sū'ērz
n. pl. (those who chase after; in Joshua, the men of Jericho hunting the spies)
Old French porsuir, from Latin prosequi, to follow after. In Scripture the pursuers are almost always searching for someone God has hidden.

Biblical Definition

Rahab hid the two spies under the stalks of flax on her roof, sent the king's men off toward the fords, and gave the spies their instructions: “Get you to the mountain, lest the pursuers meet you; and hide yourselves there three days, until the pursuers be returned: and afterward may ye go your way” (Jos 2:16). They obeyed, “and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not” (Jos 2:22). A harlot in a doomed city outwitted her own king's search parties, and she did it because she had heard what the LORD did to the Red sea and confessed, the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath. She is in Hebrews 11 among the heroes of faith and in Matthew 1 in the genealogy of Christ. The word appears once more, at Ai, where the ambush turned the battle: “the people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers” (Jos 8:20). The men of Ai had been drawn out by a feigned flight, and the moment the smoke of their city rose behind them, the fleeing men turned. In both scenes the pursuers are confident, numerous, and entirely mistaken about who is being hunted.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pursuer as one who follows with a view to overtake; one who chases; a plaintiff or prosecutor in some legal usage.

expand to see more

PURSUER, n. One who follows with a view to overtake or apprehend; one who chases.

2. In Scotland, a plaintiff; a prosecutor.

PURSUE, v.t. To follow; to go or proceed after or in a certain course; to chase.

Key Scripture

Jos 2:16 — "And she said unto them, Get you to the mountain, lest the pursuers meet you; and hide yourselves there three days, until the pursuers be returned: and afterward may ye go your way."

Jos 2:22 — "And they went, and came unto the mountain, and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not."

Jos 2:11 — "And as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath."

Modern Corruption

Rahab is treated either as an embarrassment to be explained away or as proof that Scripture excuses a lie, and both readings miss what Hebrews and James actually commend in her.

expand to see more

Rahab poses a genuine question that Christian ethics has argued for centuries: she deceived the king's pursuers, and she is commended. The two easy answers are both wrong. The first sanitises her, insisting that she cannot really have lied or that a Canaanite could not be expected to know better; the text is not embarrassed and calls her Rahab the harlot in three separate books. The second concludes that Scripture permits falsehood whenever the cause is good, which is a rule no one could safely hold and which the Bible's own condemnations of lying will not support. The New Testament tells us precisely what was commended, and it is neither her trade nor her tongue. Hebrews 11:31: by faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace. James 2:25: was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way? The commended thing is the receiving and the sending — that she threw in her lot with the people of God against her own city, at the risk of her life, on the strength of what she had heard about the Red sea. Her confession in Joshua 2:11 is better theology than most of Israel managed in the wilderness, and the scarlet line in the window is one of the plainest pictures of the passover blood in the Old Testament.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew radaph (H7291), to pursue, to chase, to persecute; baqash (H1245), to seek, to search out; tiqvah (H8615), a line or cord — the scarlet thread in the window.

expand to see more

Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, chase, or persecute; the king's men after the spies, and goodness and mercy that shall follow me all the days of my life; Joshua 2:16, Psalm 23:6.

Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, to search diligently; the pursuers sought them throughout all the way; Joshua 2:22, Jeremiah 29:13.

Hebrew tiqvah (H8615) — a cord, and also hope; the scarlet line Rahab bound in the window is the same word as the hope of Israel; Joshua 2:18, Jeremiah 29:11.

Usage

"“Lest the pursuers meet you” — a harlot directing the LORD's spies past her own king's search."

"“The pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not” — confident, numerous, and mistaken."

"“The people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers” — the ambush at Ai."
